articles.title: I went to America’s largest gathering of astrologers. It was a battle over how to read the stars
articles.summary: Now a $15bn industry, astrology is more mainstream in the US than ever. But its practitioners are still debating: who gets to have authority on the celestial bodies?“The dwarf planets change everything,” said the woman with the smart haircut as she made a mind blown gesture with her fingertips, temples to air.I am at the United Astrology Conference, the largest professional gathering of astrologers in the world, in downtown Chicago. articles.full_text:
“The dwarf planets change everything,” said the woman with the smart haircut as she made a mind blown gesture with her fingertips, temples to air.
I am at the United Astrology Conference, the largest professional gathering of astrologers in the world, in downtown Chicago. Around me, vendors are hoping to excite the 1,500 attenders, flogging books, tracts, affiliations, proprietary apps and various software programs that have replaced the laborious chart-drawing of yore.
I admit, I had come expecting a crowd flaunting amulets and sweeping cloaks. But apart from the occasional streak of purple hair and wispy wizard beard, what I encountered was an even weirder normcore of podiatry-sensible footwear and Oxford button-downs. At a glance, it could almost have been a trade convention of insurance adjusters: experts gathered to contemplate the future, assess risk, gauge the impact of events beyond our control.
In that sense, the room reflected astrology’s broader transformation. Astrology is now a $15bn industry. From the marginal, it has crept into the mainstream. A 2025 Pew Research report found that 30% of American adults consult astrology, tarot or a fortune teller at least once a year, and 43% of women under 50 claim to “believe in astrology”.
But its influence on the zeitgeist has hardly made astrology more settled. As I sat down with my interlocutor, her companion Alan Clay, founder of Dwarf Planet University, tells me the mainstays of the solar system can only get you so far. Recent astral discoveries, he said, have enriched the picture, offering a view into the unconscious through bodies drifting in the Kuiper belt, billions of miles beyond the sun.
On the wall behind his booth, the price of a reading has been slashed from $29 to $9.
He pulled my chart, a term that I learn carries tremendous weight, something between destiny and the template of my very being. There is the dwarf planet Makemake in my fifth house (I too, had to look this up), which carries bold implications for creative expression and, less attractively, secret or potentially bruising sexual affairs.
Some of this resonated. And therein lies the problem. Part of astrology’s current appeal is how quickly it can make itself feel personal – and persuasive.
Like any sufficiently established field, modern astrology has developed its own hierarchies, factions and grudges. There are fights over tradition and fears about AI; impatient zoomers butting heads with baffled boomers; older men with reputations for harassment; and quieter epistemic disputes. (Has no one noticed, for instance, that almost all the planets are male?)
Beneath all of it was a more fundamental question: who gets to interpret the stars?
“Astrology is the oldest of the occult sciences,” writes scholar Benson Bobrick in his 2005 history, The Fated Sky. “It is also the origin of science itself.”
For millennia, people have looked to the heavens for guidance and meaning: when to hunt and harvest, how to navigate the seas. The night presents a tapestry of gods and heroes, myths and parables. The stars are indifferent to these projections, of course, but they reveal a great deal about the people making them.
The basic premise of astrology is that the configuration of the sky at the moment of your birth leaves its imprint on your constitution and life trajectory. As above, so below. If in the past, the stars reflected a collective social order, today they are more often treated as a vast personal mirror.
The principle is straightforward. What astrologers make of it is not.
I arrived at the conference, which sold out of its advance weekend passes, with what seemed like a simple question: what does astrology mean to the practitioner in 2026? Moving from room to windowless room, I quickly realized the question was less simple than naive.
“Astrology is really an art form,” said one seasoned practitioner. “There is the technical component, but it’s mostly about understanding human behavior.”
To another, it was a spiritual practice, a means of communing with the ancients. It was unscientific, and also “not not a science”. It was a field of infinite study: “We’ll never get to the bottom of it.” It was moreover a language, composed of symbols and competing dialects, but nonetheless extant. “No one questions whether Spanish is real,” the astrologer Samuel Reynolds told me.
And yet, in one lecture I attended, Mark Jones, an astrologer and psychotherapist, opened with the controversial claim: “Astrology is not real.” At his words, a murmur rolled through the room, before he elaborated: “not in the sense that you are”. By his telling, the planets exert their influence on the psyche through a theory of object relations. He clicked through slides, and spoke with great authority on the spatial impact of Neptune and the role of the moon in the developmental self.
But that notwithstanding, he said: “The single biggest problem astrologers have is that they believe in astrology too much.”
Just what to believe in and what methods to follow are open and contentious questions. “There are as many branches of astrology as there are astrologers,” one attender told me, before rattling off a list. There’s horary astrology, an oracle for a single moment – is the person I made eyes with on the subway someone special? – and electional astrology, dealing with the timing of events (one woman told me that, much to the chagrin of her friends and family, her chart dictated a 7.30am wedding.)
There’s also evolutionary astrology, which maps the soul over lifetimes; mundane astrology, concerning politics and society; and medical astrology. It goes on: relational, predictive, Jungian (the Jungian vibes are strong).
Above all, it was presented to me as a kind of security blanket: a system for understanding the inexplicable, a way to make sense of a shitty day, a means to grasp the contours of current upheavals and find solace in their eventual end. During Covid, one astrologer explained: “People were really looking for answers. They were like, ‘Sky, tell me what’s going on.’”
The 185 experts who presented were doing what people at conferences do: establishing hierarchies and professionalizing a crowded, competitive field. A conference, after all, is an occasion for conferring legitimacy and codifying the rules of the trade.
In astrology, this raises some obvious complications. If you are claiming to see something about a person’s future, what are you responsible for telling them?
Some clients, I was told, “just want the good stuff”. Other practitioners prefer to rip off the Band-Aid – if dark days lie ahead, it’s better to make an ominous prognostication so the afflicted can prepare or hunker down as necessary.
But what happens when you get it wrong?
“There is no wrong,” Clay told me. “There are different interpretations. Right or wrong is a Saturnian construct, it’s useful but doesn’t help us understand these new energies.”
That is not, however, the abiding consensus. One of the conference seminars was devoted to learning from readings that went awry.
“When people are giving predictions, there is at least a five or 10% chance that it’s not right, and the stakes are huge,” said Kay Taylor, president of the UAC and the Organization for Professional Astrology.
Another astrologer illustrated the stakes with a story from her own practice. Based on her reading of a client’s chart, she concluded that both of the client’s parents would die within the year. She felt obliged to convey this information, whereupon the client quit their job and moved across the country to be with their parents for the end.
“But they didn’t die!” She exclaimed with surprising pride.
That was years ago. Mom and dad are still alive and well. Yet the astrologer assured me that even though the prediction was off, the message remained sound. Her client got to enjoy some bonus time with her parents.
Gaffes like this are what make training critical, I was told. No fewer than six professional organizations were sponsoring this year’s gathering – the National Council for Geocosmic Research is the only one without “astrology” in its name – and they offered various routes to affiliated credentialing and curricula, ranging from astrological markers of ADHD to advanced training in asteroids.
Celeste Nash-Weninger, from the American Federation of Astrologers, told me: “Every person is a complicated mathematical formula.” She used to be intimidated by the graphs and numbers, but after taking recommended courses – “and they’re tough: eight hours of math and delineation” – she has confidence in “how the heavens move”.
Whether advanced math is required for mastery is open to debate. But there is one thing nearly everyone here agrees on: technology has made astrology more accessible – but also, some practitioners worry, diluted its expertise.
“Before, people had to do it all by hand,” said Leslie Benson, an astrologer who works for AstroGraph, maker of the popular TimePassages app. “You had to have an ephemeris, where you looked up every placement. You had to draw it all. Now it’s instant.”
Most have eagerly embraced the new tools; after all, if software can do the calculations, practitioners have more time for the interpretive work. But they also remove one of the barriers by which skill was once recognized.
Artificial intelligence is where most everyone here draws the line. Of course, AI was inevitable: Pluto is in Aquarius and Uranus is in Gemini – yikes – but the contemporary astrologer, at least according to one seminar, must safeguard the personal and spiritual component of the work. “Embracing Uranus,” it advised, referring to the dark trickster of the cosmos, “without losing your soul.”
Co-Star, the astrology app that has brought personalized charts and algorithmic readings to millions of users, is notably absent from the conference, and attenders clucked in disapproval over news of its recent acquisition by the AI startup Midjourney. The technology that made astrology

articles.title: Tech in cars can be used to snoop on you, Dutch spy chiefs warn
articles.summary: Hostile states could access cameras, microphones or GPS, says intelligence agency amid concerns over Chinese importsDrivers have been warned that the smart features built into modern cars such as microphones, cameras and GPS trackers could be used by hostile states to spy on them.The Dutch General Intelligence and Security Service (AIVD) called for “awareness of espionage risks around modern vehicles”, including microphones that can by switched on remotely to listen to conversations. articles.full_text:
Drivers have been warned that the smart features built into modern cars such as microphones, cameras and GPS trackers could be used by hostile states to spy on them.
The Dutch General Intelligence and Security Service (AIVD) called for “awareness of espionage risks around modern vehicles”, including microphones that can by switched on remotely to listen to conversations.
It did not mention an individual country, but the warning will add to concerns around a recent boom in Chinese car imports into the UK.
In a translated document released on Wednesday, the AIVD said cars were becoming “increasingly smart” with digital systems that collected data and connected to the internet.
“On the one hand this offers practical benefits, but on the other hand these systems collect a great deal of data about occupants, the vehicle itself, and about objects and people in the vicinity. Various parties, including state actors, can gain access to this data,” it added.
The alert follows reports last year that British defence firms working for the UK government had cautioned staff against connecting or pairing their phones with Chinese-made electric cars, owing to fears that Beijing could extract sensitive data from the devices.
Chinese-owned brands now account for 15% of all new cars registered in the UK, according to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders, almost 175,000 vehicles in the first half of 2026 and more than double the same period last year.
Models by MG, BYD and Jaecoo, whose parent company Chery is part-owned by the Chinese state, have led the surge, popular for their low price and in-car technology. The Jaecoo 7 was the UK’s bestselling car in March.
MPs have raised concerns that China’s national intelligence law requires its companies to assist the state’s intelligence services when requested.
The UK Ministry of Defence has said it is working with other government departments “to understand and mitigate any potential threats to national security” from vehicles.
This year, the MoD reportedly banned cars with Chinese parts from sensitive military sites, including RAF Wyton in Cambridgeshire and the Dorset headquarters of Britain’s maritime special forces, the SBS.
The AIVD said it was “technically possible to activate” microphones and cameras remotely in some cars, allowing malicious actors to “eavesdrop on conversations” and “make recordings in and around the vehicle”.
The agency added that drivers should “not hold confidential conversations in or around the vehicle”, or “use a vehicle with an external camera when travelling to a sensitive location”.
It also said connecting phones and other devices, either via Bluetooth, wifi or charging systems could allow malicious actors to “extract data from connected devices via the vehicle”. The AIVD suggested systems such as GPS navigation systems, telematics modules and charging stations could all be used to gather and send data about the car and drivers’ whereabouts elsewhere.
On Wednesday, MI5 issued a rare public warning to UK universities to stop working with the China General Technology Research Institute, which it said was being used as a front by Beijing’s intelligence service to pay for research by UK academics and steal the secrets of hi-tech projects.
The Chinese embassy in London issued a strongly worded rebuttal, describing the accusations as “imaginary and purely fabricated”.
